verses.note: Before Israel has a tabernacle, priesthood, or law code, God gives it a calendar. Worship begins with the ordering of time around what God has done, so that the year itself becomes a confession of redemption.

Worship is described with the same word as slavery, but the master has changed. The exodus is not freedom from all service but release into the service of the God who frees, which is why the ritual of remembrance is itself called avodah.
Worship is placed where God chooses to make his name known, and its goal is his coming to bless. The altar is not a way to summon God but a place where he promises to meet his people.
The feasts gather harvest and history into one act of worship. Israel's thanksgiving for grain is also a remembrance of rescue, so that the rhythm of the farming year keeps the exodus in view.

The renewed covenant ends with the ordinary details of offering: the right bread, the right timing, the best of the harvest. Faithfulness to God is expressed in small acts of worship repeated every year.

The day ends not with the removal of sin but with burnt offerings, the gift of the whole animal to God. Cleansing opens the way to renewed worship, and the priest returns to his ordinary service in his ordinary robes.

The remedy for private, unregulated sacrifice is not to forbid eating meat but to bring it to God's house as a peace offering. Worship is gathered to the place and the mediation God appoints, and the meal itself becomes fellowship with him.
Fear, service, and oath cover the inward stance, the outward practice, and the public commitment of worship. All three are reserved for the LORD.

The phrase that describes the Levites' status becomes, in the Psalms, a prayer any believer can make. Psalm 16:5 and 73:26 call the LORD the speaker's portion, taking the Levites' privilege as a picture of what God is to every faithful person.
God is enjoyed as a possession, not only obeyed as a master. The Levites' status becomes a model for every believer, as in Psalm 73:26 and Lamentations 3:24.
God's throne among his people is their praise. The sufferer, who cannot now praise, remembers where God is found, and the psalm will end with him restored to that praise (verses 22-25).

No offering is adequate to God, not even the whole of Lebanon on the altar. Worship cannot enlarge him; it can only acknowledge him, which is the point of Psalm 50:9-12 and of Paul's words in Athens that God is not served by human hands as though he needed anything (Acts 17:25).
Restoration is not complete when people are back on their land; it is complete when they are gathered before God together. The first thing the reunited people do is go up to worship.

Worship offered while a brother's grievance is ignored is out of order. Jesus stands in the prophets' tradition that God does not want sacrifice without justice and mercy (Hosea 6:6; Amos 5:21-24), which Matthew quotes twice (9:13; 12:7).
The verse locates the value of devotion in the one it is offered to. The same act of prayer or giving can be worship of God or a bid for human praise, and the difference is invisible from outside.

Fasting is presented as a normal part of devotion to God (‘when you fast’), not an optional extra; Jesus later says his disciples will fast when the bridegroom is taken away (9:15). Its value lies in being directed to the Father.

By the time of Paul and Luke, Christians gathered and collected gifts on ‘the first day of the week’ (1 Corinthians 16:2, Acts 20:7), and John calls it ‘the Lord's day’ (Revelation 1:10). The verse is where that practice begins: Christian worship moved to Sunday because of what the women found on it.

Luke has taken care to show that worship belongs to God alone (4:8). When the disciples now worship Jesus, and Luke records it without correction, the Gospel's last scene confesses what the creeds later state: the risen Son shares the honor due to God.
The first believers kept worshiping at the temple and ate together at home. Their praise of God is joyful and daily, tied to ordinary meals as well as to the temple's hours of prayer.
Trust is itself worship. To believe that God is able to do what he promised is to give him the glory the rest of humanity withheld.
The end of reconciliation is joy in God himself, not only in his gifts. The boast that was excluded in 3:27 is restored, redirected from self to God.
Paul's teaching on the resurrection ends in thanks, not speculation. The proper response to doctrine is praise to the God who gives what we could never achieve.

The letter's theology begins as praise. Election, redemption, and the gift of the Spirit are first of all reasons to bless God, and the refrain ‘to the praise of His glory’ (verses 6, 12, 14) keeps the whole sentence pointed toward worship.
What the temple barrier prevented, Gentiles approaching God, is now open to both groups equally. Worship is defined by access through Christ, not by a place or an ethnic boundary.
Angels are commanded to worship the Son. Since Scripture reserves worship for God alone, and Revelation 22:8-9 has an angel refusing it, the verse places the Son on the side of God.
The risen Jesus leads his people's praise. Christian worship is pictured as the Son singing to the Father in the midst of his brothers and sisters, not merely as people singing about him.

What was once restricted to the high priest once a year (Leviticus 16:2) is now the ordinary privilege of God's people. The verse reshapes worship around access through Christ rather than through a sanctuary on earth.
The first covenant's worship was God-given, regulated in detail. Hebrews does not treat it as human invention to be despised but as a divinely ordered pattern whose meaning is now disclosed.
The goal of cleansing is service: ‘to serve the living God’. Forgiveness is not an end in itself but admission to the priestly worship that Israel's priests alone once offered.
The second beast is religion put in the service of power. It does not demand worship for itself but for the first beast, which is what makes it dangerous: counterfeit worship can look like a lamb.
